questions.q: The English word 'empire' comes from the Latin word 'imperium'. What does 'imperium' mean?
questions.a: 'Imperium' means 'supreme power'.

questions.q:
Match each word in Column I with its meaning in Column II.
Column I: 1. samraj  2. adhiraja  3. rajadhiraja  4. imperium
Column II: P. overlord  Q. king of kings  R. supreme power  S. the lord of all
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: samraj = the lord of all (or supreme ruler); adhiraja = overlord; rajadhiraja = king of kings; imperium = supreme power.

questions.q: Four records come from the same ancient region. Which one shows a ruler acting as a TRIBUTARY of an emperor?
o: A hill chief goes on ruling his own valley and every year sends the emperor 300 cattle and a chest of gold as a sign of loyalty
A governor appointed by a distant overlord manages a far-off province on the overlord's behalf
A province whose old ruling family was removed is now run directly by the emperor's own officials
A cloth merchant pays a fee at the city gate so that he can sell his goods in the market
questions.a: The hill chief who keeps ruling his own valley and sends cattle and gold to the emperor every year as a sign of loyalty is a tributary: he has submitted to the emperor and pays tribute. The governor is a satrap, an official, and the province run by the emperor's officials has no ruler of its own.

questions.q: True or False? 'According to the chapter, the last empire that ruled the Subcontinent existed less than a century ago.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says Indian history is full of empires that rose, expanded, declined and disappeared, and that the last empire that ruled the Subcontinent existed less than a century ago.
s: States the verdict: True
Explains that, by the chapter, the last of India's many empires to rule the Subcontinent existed less than a century ago

questions.q: (a) What is a tributary, in the sense the chapter uses? (b) Which word does the chapter give as a synonym for 'tributary'?
questions.a: (a) A tributary is a ruler or a state that has submitted to an emperor and pays him tribute, such as money, gold, grain, livestock or elephants, as a sign of submission, loyalty or respect. (b) Vassal.
s: (a) A ruler or state that has submitted to an emperor and pays him tribute
(b) Names 'vassal'

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) What does the word 'posterity' mean? (b) According to the chapter's list of the features of an empire, name two things that an emperor makes or issues. (c) From where does the emperor rule the whole territory, and what kind of place is it usually?
questions.a: (a) The generations to come. (b) Any two of: laws, currencies, weights and measures. (c) From a capital, which is usually a major centre of economic and administrative power.
s: (a) States: the generations to come
(b) Names any two of laws, currencies, weights and measures
(c) States the capital, usually a major centre of economic and administrative power

questions.q:
Class 7 of a school in Nagpur is writing a play about an imaginary emperor, Vikramaditya, whose capital is the city of Suvarnapur. In the script, his officials collect taxes and keep law and order in every province, his workers build roads between the towns, his treasury pays for a centre of learning where poets and scholars meet, and his soldiers guard the borders against attacks from outside. Read the script and answer.
(a) Which feature of an empire does the centre of learning for poets and scholars show?
(b) For which purpose of an emperor's army, from the chapter's list, are the soldiers on the borders used?
(c) Which feature of an empire do the officials who collect taxes and keep law and order show?
(d) Which feature of an empire do the roads between the towns show?
questions.a: (a) The emperor encourages art, literature, religions, schools of thought and centres of learning. (b) To protect the empire from outside aggression. (c) The emperor designs and maintains an administration, with officials to manage the territories, collect taxes and keep law and order. (d) The emperor maintains communication networks and other infrastructure for administration, trade and people's welfare.
s: (a) Names the feature: encouraging art, literature and centres of learning
(b) States: protecting the empire from outside aggression
(c) Names the feature: an administration with officials to collect taxes and keep law and order
(d) Names the feature: communication networks and infrastructure such as roads

questions.q:
A student writes: 'Every empire is made by war and kept going only by war.' Evaluate this claim using the chapter.
(a) How does the chapter say a powerful ruler usually came to exert power over smaller kingdoms?
(b) After seeing the death and destruction of the Kalinga war, what did Ashoka choose?
(c) What does the chapter say a well-managed empire could do for the smaller kingdoms inside it?
(d) Using (a) and (b), judge the first half of the claim: is every empire made by war?
(e) Using (b) and (c), judge the second half: is an empire kept going only by war? Then give your overall verdict on the claim.
questions.a: (a) Often after waging war against the smaller kingdoms. (b) He chose to give up violence and, to the greatest extent possible, follow the Buddha's path of peace and non-violence. (c) It could bring political unity, reduce or end warfare among the smaller kingdoms, and lead to greater prosperity than smaller, warring kingdoms. (d) Largely supported but overstated: rulers gained power 'often' after war, and even Ashoka had first expanded his empire and fought at Kalinga, but 'often' is not 'every'. (e) Not supported: the chapter does say empires were usually maintained through force and repression, but Ashoka went on ruling his vast empire after choosing peace and caring for his subjects' welfare, and a well-managed empire could reduce warfare and bring prosperity, so war was not the only means. Overall the claim is partly right: war very often made empires, but 'every' and 'only' go too far.
s: (a) States: often after waging war against the smaller kingdoms
(b) States that Ashoka gave up violence and chose the path of peace and non-violence
(c) States political unity, less or no warfare among the kingdoms, or greater prosperity
(d) Judges the first half as largely supported but overstated ('often', not 'every'), with evidence from (a) or (b)
(e) Judges the second half as not supported, weighing the chapter's 'force and repression' against (b) and (c), and gives the verdict 'partly right'

questions.q: What were the guilds of traders, craftsmen, moneylenders or agriculturists called in ancient India?
questions.a: Guilds were called shrenis.

questions.q:
Read the statements about guilds in ancient India.
I. As far as evidence shows, a guild had a head who was usually elected.
II. The king made the internal rules of each guild and changed them as he wished.
III. Guilds lasted only a few years and were found in a small area of India.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only statement I is correct. Guilds had the autonomy to make their own rules and the king was not to interfere, and guilds spread over large parts of India and endured for centuries.

questions.q: (a) Name the two main trade routes marked on the chapter's map of trade routes from about 500 BCE onward. (b) Name any two kinds of goods that were among the main items of trade in ancient India.
questions.a: (a) The Uttarapatha and the Dakshinapatha. (b) Any two of: textiles, spices, agricultural produce, gems and other luxury items, handicraft products, animals.
s: (a) Names the Uttarapatha and the Dakshinapatha
(b) Names two traded goods from the chapter, such as textiles and spices

questions.q:
King Surasena plans to keep a large army to guard his empire. Answer each part in one or two lines.
(a) Name two things his soldiers need besides weapons.
(b) The chapter says all this requires considerable economic power. Name one more thing it says maintaining an army requires.
(c) Which kind of economic activity does the chapter call one of the keys to maintaining an empire?
(d) If more goods are traded, what does this mean for the producers?
(e) What does more trade mean for the ruler?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: food, clothes, pay. (b) Either control over the workforce or access to resources. (c) Production and trade. (d) More income for the producers. (e) Increased tax collections for the ruler.
s: (a) Names two needs of soldiers: food, clothes or pay
(b) Names control over the workforce or access to resources
(c) Names production and trade
(d) States more income for the producers
(e) States more tax collections for the ruler

questions.q: Raju says: 'Guilds stopped existing long ago, so they tell us nothing about Indian society and have no link with life in India today.' Is he right? Give a verdict and two reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. (1) The chapter says that even after guilds ceased to exist formally, their spirit continued to influence India's trade and business, sometimes even to this day. (2) Guilds are an excellent example of the self-organising abilities of Indian society, like the ancient village unit with its committees and councils, so they do tell us about Indian society.
s: Verdict: No, he is not right
States that the spirit of guilds continued to influence trade and business, sometimes to this day
States that guilds show the self-organising ability of Indian society (like the village unit with its councils)

questions.q:
Assertion (A): According to the chapter, guilds in ancient India had the autonomy to make their own internal rules.
Reason (R): As an ancient text put it, cultivators, traders, herdsmen, moneylenders and artisans had authority to lay down rules for their own classes, and the king was not to interfere with them.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: because these groups had the authority to lay down rules for their own classes, without interference from the king, guilds could make their own internal rules.

questions.q:
In an imaginary river-port town of the Maurya age, the potters' guild has 50 members and an elected head. Last year its members sold 9,000 pots. This year the head changed the guild's rules so that only his own relatives may sell at the busy river ghat; sales fell to 6,300 pots, and 15 members complained to the king's officer that the guild no longer listens to them. The officer must decide whether to step in.
(a) Who usually led a guild, and what were its executive officers supposed to have?
(b) By what percentage did the guild's sales fall?
(c) The chapter gives a condition under which a ruler should NOT interfere with local institutions. State it.
(d) Using only the condition in (c) and your answer to (b), is the condition for the ruler to stay out met here? Say what this means for the officer.
questions.a: (a) A guild had a head, who was usually elected, and executive officers who were supposed to have all kinds of ethical qualities. (b) Sales fell by 9,000 - 6,300 = 2,700 pots; 2,700 / 9,000 x 100 = 30%. (c) An enlightened ruler lets people organise themselves and refrains from interfering if the local institutions work satisfactorily (and the king need not interfere with guilds while trade flourishes). (d) No: the condition is that the local institution works satisfactorily, but sales have fallen by 30% and members are shut out, so the guild is not working satisfactorily; the condition for staying out is not met, so the officer may step in, though only to restore fair rules that the guild then runs itself.
s: (a) States an elected head and executive officers expected to have ethical qualities
(b) Computes a fall of 2,700 pots, that is 30%
(c) States that a ruler should not interfere if local institutions work satisfactorily (or while trade flourishes)
(d) States that the condition is not met because of the 30% fall (and shut-out members), so the officer may step in

questions.q: Magadha, the kingdom that set the stage for India's first empire, lay in which present-day region?
o: South Bihar and some adjoining areas
questions.a: Magadha lay in modern-day south Bihar and some adjoining areas.

questions.q: Which two rivers gave Magadha a geographical advantage for trade because they could be used for transport?
questions.a: The Ganga and the Son rivers.

questions.q: True or False? 'Mahapadma Nanda was the last emperor of the Nanda dynasty.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Mahapadma Nanda founded the Nanda dynasty around the 5th century BCE; its last emperor was Dhana Nanda.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: Mahapadma Nanda founded the dynasty and Dhana Nanda was its last emperor

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) Name the early king who played a crucial role in making Magadha a dominant centre of power. (b) Name the two famed religious figures who lived in his time. (c) Name the famed Sanskrit grammarian who lived in the time of the Nandas, and the text he composed.
questions.a: (a) Ajatashatru. (b) Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha) and Vardhamana (Mahavira). (c) Panini, who composed the Ashtadhyayi.
s: (a) Names Ajatashatru
(b) Names the Buddha and Mahavira
(c) Names Panini and the Ashtadhyayi

questions.q:
Match each resource of Magadha in Column I with the use the chapter gives for it in Column II.
Column I: 1. Forests  2. Iron ore from the nearby hills  3. The Ganga and Son rivers  4. Fertile land of the Ganga plains
Column II: P. Ploughs and sharper weapons  Q. Timber and elephants  R. Transport for trade  S. Surplus food grains
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Forests gave timber and elephants; iron ore gave ploughs and sharper weapons; the Ganga and Son gave transport for trade; the fertile land gave surplus food grains.

questions.q: Using the chapter's meaning of an empire, which fact about Mahapadma Nanda best shows that Magadha under him had become an empire and not just a large kingdom?
o: He unified many smaller kingdoms and extended his rule across parts of eastern and northern India
He began issuing coins as the economy thrived, showing his economic power
Greek accounts say that his dynasty maintained a large army
He ruled from Magadha, in the resource-rich Ganga plains with fertile land and forests
questions.a: He unified many smaller kingdoms and extended his rule across parts of eastern and northern India: an empire is a collection of smaller kingdoms or territories under one powerful ruler. Coins, a large army or a rich homeland could belong to a large kingdom too.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Mahapadma Nanda began issuing coins.
Reason (R): Greek accounts tell us that the Nanda dynasty maintained a large army.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: Mahapadma Nanda began issuing coins as the economy thrived, to demonstrate his economic power; the large army is a separate fact about the Nandas' strength.

questions.q:
Two imaginary kingdoms of the 6th century BCE want to grow into an empire. Nadipur lies on a fertile plain with thick forests full of timber and wild elephants, and a wide river that boats use all year; it has no iron ore and must buy iron from a far-off kingdom. Lohagiri has rich iron ore in its hills, but its soil is thin and rocky, it has only scrubland with no large forests or elephants, and its streams dry up in summer and are too shallow for boats.
(a) The chapter names five natural advantages of Magadha: fertile land, forests for timber, elephants, iron ore and rivers for transport. How many of these does each kingdom have?
(b) Which advantage does Lohagiri have that Nadipur lacks, and what two things did it do for Magadha?
(c) How could Nadipur's river help it make up for having no iron of its own?
(d) Which kingdom is more likely to grow into an empire? Judge, and say why the count in (a) alone does not settle it.
questions.a: (a) Nadipur has 4 (fertile land, forests, elephants, a river for transport); Lohagiri has 1 (iron ore). (b) Iron ore: in Magadha iron ploughs increased agricultural produce, and lighter, sharper iron weapons strengthened the army. (c) Rivers could be used for transportation, which gave an advantage for trade; trade boosts income, so Nadipur could bring in iron by boat and pay for it. (d) Either kingdom can be argued if the advantages are weighed. For example: Nadipur, since it has food, timber, elephants and a river for trade, and can buy iron; but a count treats all advantages as equal, while iron served both farming and war, and Nadipur depends on a far-off supplier. Or: Lohagiri, since iron ore proved crucial for the expansion of a kingdom, though its poor soil and lack of river transport hold it back.
s: (a) Counts 4 for Nadipur and 1 for Lohagiri
(b) Names iron ore: iron ploughs raised produce and iron weapons strengthened the army
(c) Explains that river transport allows trade, through which iron can be brought in and paid for
(d) Reaches a decision for either kingdom that weighs iron against food, forests and transport, and says why the count alone does not settle it

questions.q: Which king of the Pauravas did Alexander defeat in Punjab?
questions.a: Alexander defeated Porus, king of the Pauravas, in Punjab.

questions.q: (a) From which region did Alexander come? (b) Where did he die, and at what age?
questions.a: (a) Macedonia (he was a Greek king from Macedonia). (b) He died in Babylon at the age of 32.
s: (a) Names Macedonia
(b) Names Babylon and the age of 32

questions.q: Who were the satraps of the Persian and Greek empires?
o: Governors of provinces left behind by the overlord to manage far-off territories
Kings who paid tribute but were never governed by the overlord
Elected heads of guilds of traders and craftsmen
Indian sages who answered Alexander's riddles
questions.a: Satraps were governors of provinces left behind by the overlord, such as Alexander, to manage far-off territories.

questions.q: True or False? 'Alexander turned back from India because Porus defeated him in Punjab.' Give the verdict and the correct reason for the retreat.
questions.a: False. Alexander defeated Porus. He turned back because, after fierce resistance from local tribes and rulers, his tired and homesick soldiers lost the will to fight and refused to move deeper into India towards the Ganga.
s: States the verdict: False, Alexander defeated Porus
Gives the real reason: tired, homesick soldiers refused to go on towards the Ganga after fierce resistance

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) What did Alexander do to the population of several cities in India when he met fierce resistance from local tribes and rulers? (b) What does the Greek coin shown in the chapter probably show? (c) What did Alexander face when he got back to Persia?
questions.a: (a) He massacred the population of several cities. (b) Alexander on horseback attacking Porus on his elephant. (c) Rebellions and political turmoil.
s: (a) States that he massacred the population of several cities
(b) States: Alexander on horseback attacking Porus on his elephant
(c) States rebellions and political turmoil

questions.q:
Read the statements about Alexander's campaign in India.
I. Greek records mention that in a few battles in India, women fought side by side with their men.
II. After defeating Porus, Alexander removed him and placed a Greek general at the head of his kingdom.
III. The northwestern region where Porus ruled lay along an ancient route connecting to the Mediterranean.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements I and III are correct. Statement II is wrong: when Porus asked to be treated 'like a King', Alexander left Porus himself at the head of his kingdom, as satrap.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Alexander's army did not march deeper into India towards the Ganga.
Reason (R): Alexander himself was seriously wounded in a battle in India.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: the chapter says the army stopped because the tired and homesick soldiers lost the will to fight and refused to move deeper into India, not because of Alexander's wound.

questions.q:
A museum is planning a panel called 'The Satraps Alexander Left Behind'. Its notes say: Alexander, eager to reach the 'end of the world', built an empire that spread over three continents. Satraps were governors left behind by an overlord to manage far-off territories, and they had significant power and freedom despite being mere officials. After Alexander died, his empire was soon divided. Around 321 BCE the Maurya Empire emerged in Magadha, and Chandragupta Maurya, advised by Kautilya, later defeated the Greek satraps left in the northwest.
(a) Using the chapter's reasons why a king wants to turn his kingdom into an empire, give one thing Alexander would have gained from ruling over the 'entire world'.
(b) Using the notes, explain why a satrap could hold such power and freedom although he was a mere official.
(c) The satraps had 'significant power and freedom', yet Chandragupta defeated them. Give one advantage he had that came from Magadha itself.
(d) Give one other advantage Chandragupta had, and say what a satrap ruling one far-off province lacked by comparison.
questions.a: (a) Any one: being remembered by the generations to come; control of large areas and access to their resources to build economic and military strength; great wealth. (b) He managed a far-off territory, very far from the overlord, who could not easily watch or control him in an empire spread over three continents. (c) Magadha's geographical advantages, its established economic system or its flourishing trade. (d) The advice of Kautilya, a master strategist, or the large base of the Nanda territories he had absorbed; a satrap had only one far-off province and, once Alexander's empire was divided, no larger empire or such a base behind him.
s: (a) Gives one gain from the chapter's list: fame for posterity, resources for economic and military strength, or great wealth
(b) Explains that the satrap's territory was far from the overlord, who could not easily control it
(c) Names Magadha's geography, established economic system or flourishing trade
(d) Names Kautilya's advice or the absorbed Nanda territories and contrasts it with a satrap's single far-off province

questions.q: Around which year did Chandragupta Maurya found the Maurya Empire?
questions.a: Around 321 BCE.

questions.q: True or False? 'Kautilya vowed to end the Nanda rule because Chandragupta asked him to help win the throne.' Give the verdict and the corrected reason.
questions.a: False. Kautilya advised Dhana Nanda to change his ways; angered, Dhana Nanda insulted Kautilya and threw him out of his court, and this led to Kautilya's vow to end the Nanda rule.
s: States the verdict: False
Gives the real reason: Dhana Nanda insulted Kautilya and threw him out of his court

questions.q: (a) Give the two other names by which Kautilya is sometimes known. (b) According to Buddhist texts, where did he teach?
questions.a: (a) Chanakya and Vishnugupta. (b) At the world-renowned university of Takshashila (modern-day Taxila).
s: (a) Names Chanakya and Vishnugupta
(b) Names Takshashila (Taxila)

questions.q:
Match each person in Column I with the description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Kautilya  2. Megasthenes  3. Dhana Nanda  4. Chandragupta Maurya
Column II: P. The rich but unpopular last Nanda emperor  Q. Founder of the Maurya Empire, with Pataliputra as capital  R. Mentor and master strategist  S. Greek historian and diplomat who wrote Indika
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Kautilya was the mentor and master strategist; Megasthenes the Greek historian and diplomat who wrote Indika; Dhana Nanda the rich but unpopular last Nanda emperor; Chandragupta Maurya the founder of the Maurya Empire with Pataliputra as capital.

questions.q:
Read the statements about Chandragupta Maurya's rule.
I. He made Pataliputra his capital after taking control of Magadha.
II. His empire stretched from the northern plains to the Deccan plateau.
III. After defeating the Greeks he kept a diplomatic relationship with them.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: All three statements are correct.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Historians today cannot read Megasthenes' Indika as a complete book.
Reason (R): Indika was lost, except for some excerpts quoted by later Greek scholars.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the book cannot be read whole because it was lost, and only the excerpts quoted by later Greek scholars survive.

questions.q:
A school drama club writes a four-scene play called 'The Rise of Chandragupta'. Scene 1: Kautilya teaches students at Takshashila. Scene 2: Dhana Nanda thanks Kautilya warmly for his advice and makes him a minister. Scene 3: Chandragupta is crowned and announces Takshashila as the capital of his new empire. Scene 4: Megasthenes, a Greek diplomat, arrives at court while Chandragupta is still at war with the Greek satraps.
Check each scene against the chapter.
(a) Scene 1  (b) Scene 2  (c) Scene 3  (d) Scene 4
For each, say whether it fits the chapter, and correct it if it does not.
questions.a: (a) Fits: according to Buddhist texts Kautilya was a teacher at Takshashila. (b) Wrong: Dhana Nanda was angered by the advice, insulted Kautilya and threw him out of his court. (c) Wrong: Chandragupta took control of Magadha and made Pataliputra his capital. (d) Wrong order: Chandragupta hosted Megasthenes after he had defeated the Greeks, when he kept a diplomatic relationship with them.
s: (a) Judges Scene 1 correct: Kautilya taught at Takshashila
(b) Corrects Scene 2: Dhana Nanda insulted Kautilya and threw him out
(c) Corrects Scene 3: the capital was Pataliputra
(d) Corrects Scene 4: Megasthenes came after the Greeks were defeated

questions.q: In Kautilya's political thought, what is the 'saptanga'?
o: The seven parts that constitute a kingdom
The seven kings who paid tribute to the emperor
The seven guilds of a capital city
The seven rock edicts of a king
questions.a: The saptanga is the seven parts that constitute a kingdom.

questions.q:
Match each part of Kautilya's saptanga in Column I with its meaning in Column II.
Column I: 1. kosha  2. mitra  3. durga  4. janapada
Column II: P. the fortified towns and cities  Q. the territory of the state with its population  R. the treasury or wealth of the kingdom  S. the allies
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: kosha = the treasury or wealth of the kingdom; mitra = the allies; durga = the fortified towns and cities; janapada = the territory of the state with its population.

questions.q: True or False? 'According to Kautilya, the parts of a kingdom must be kept settled, protected and prosperous both through warfare and through alliances for peace, as the case may be.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. Kautilya said the saptanga together must create a settled, well-protected and prosperous kingdom, maintained both through warfare and through alliances for peace, as the case may be.
s: States the verdict: True
Explains that the saptanga is kept up by warfare or by alliances for peace, as the case demands

questions.q: Give the meaning of each of these parts of Kautilya's saptanga in one line. (a) swami (b) amatya (c) danda
questions.a: (a) Swami is the king. (b) Amatya is the group of councillors, ministers and other high officials. (c) Danda is the forces of defence and of law and order.
s: (a) Swami: the king
(b) Amatya: the councillors, ministers and other high officials
(c) Danda: the forces of defence and law and order

questions.q: King Dhruvasen of an imaginary kingdom issues many strict laws against theft and cheating in markets, but he appoints only two officers for the whole kingdom to see that the laws are obeyed and offenders punished. (a) According to Kautilya, what did law and order in society need? (b) Using that idea, explain why Dhruvasen's laws are unlikely to bring order.
questions.a: (a) Kautilya said law and order in society necessitated a strong administration. (b) Laws work only if officials carry them out and punish those who break them; two officers cannot do this across a whole kingdom, so the administration is weak and the laws stay on paper.
s: (a) States that law and order needed a strong administration
(b) Explains that two officers make the administration too weak to enforce the laws and punish offenders

questions.q:
A class compares Kautilya's saptanga with a modern nation, as the chapter suggests. Match each modern feature in Column I with the saptanga part in Column II that it is most like.
Column I: 1. The Council of Ministers and senior officers  2. The army and the police  3. Friendly countries that sign treaties with the nation  4. The land of the nation and its citizens
Column II: P. danda  Q. janapada  R. amatya  S. mitra
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Ministers and senior officers are like amatya; the army and police like danda (forces of defence and law and order); friendly countries like mitra (allies); the land and its citizens like janapada (territory with its population).

questions.q: The treasury (kosha) of an imaginary kingdom receives 10 lakh coins a year: 6 lakh from farm taxes in the countryside, 3 lakh from taxes on trade and 1 lakh as tribute. (a) What percentage of the income comes from the countryside? (b) A drought halves the farm taxes, and the other two incomes stay the same. What is the new yearly income, and by what percentage has it fallen? (c) Which two parts of the saptanga are hit first by this drought? (d) Which saying of Kautilya does this example support? (e) Using your answers, explain why Kautilya wanted the king to care for the welfare of the countryside.
questions.a: (a) 6 / 10 = 60 percent. (b) Farm taxes fall to 3 lakh, so income is 3 + 3 + 1 = 7 lakh, a fall of 3 lakh, which is 30 percent. (c) The janapada (the territory and its people, the farmers) and the kosha (the treasury). (d) That a king should increase his power by promoting the welfare of his people, for power comes from the countryside, the source of all economic activity. (e) Most of the treasury depends on the countryside, so when farmers suffer the treasury shrinks by nearly a third; caring for the countryside keeps the treasury, and so the king's power, strong.
s: (a) Computes 60 percent
(b) Computes 7 lakh and a 30 percent fall
(c) Names janapada and kosha
(d) Quotes or states Kautilya's idea that power comes from the countryside
(e) Explains that welfare of the countryside protects the treasury and the king's power

questions.q:
A report on the imaginary kingdom of Sumeru reads: 'Our neighbour Kalapur has an army of 30,000 and may attack. Our own army has 18,000 soldiers. Of our 4 forts, 3 are in good repair. Last year we had 5 allies, but 3 have made peace with Kalapur; only 2 remain, and each has promised 4,000 soldiers. The treasury holds 3 lakh coins. Repairing the fourth fort costs 2 lakh coins. Gifts and treaties to win back 2 of the lost allies, each of whom would also send 4,000 soldiers, cost 3 lakh coins. We cannot do both.'
(a) Which two parts of the saptanga are these two choices about?
(b) What percentage of its allies has Sumeru lost, and what percentage of its forts are in good repair?
(c) How many soldiers can Sumeru field with its 2 remaining allies, and how many if 2 more allies are won back? Compare each with Kalapur's army.
(d) Should the 3 lakh coins go to the fort or to the allies? Decide, using (b), (c) and Kautilya's idea of how a kingdom is maintained.
questions.a: (a) The fort is durga (fortified towns and cities); the allies are mitra. (b) Allies lost: 3 / 5 = 60%; forts in good repair: 3 / 4 = 75%. (c) With 2 allies: 18,000 + 2 x 4,000 = 26,000, fewer than Kalapur's 30,000; with 4 allies: 18,000 + 4 x 4,000 = 34,000, more than 30,000. (d) The allies: the mitra is the weaker part (60% lost, while 75% of the forts are sound), and winning back two allies turns a 26,000 to 30,000 shortfall into a 34,000 to 30,000 lead; Kautilya said a kingdom is maintained both through warfare and through alliances, as the case may be.
s: (a) Names durga for the fort and mitra for the allies
(b) Computes 60% of allies lost and 75% of forts in good repair
(c) Computes 26,000 (below 30,000) and 34,000 (above 30,000)
(d) Chooses the allies, using the weaker mitra and the 34,000 to 30,000 comparison, linked to Kautilya's warfare-and-alliances idea

questions.q: Ashoka waged a ferocious war that changed the path of his life. Where was it fought?
questions.a: In Kalinga, modern-day Odisha.

questions.q: In which language were most of Ashoka's edicts inscribed?
questions.a: Most of the edicts were in Prakrit (written in the Brahmi script).

questions.q: (a) What is an edict? (b) What is an emissary? Name one place to which Ashoka sent emissaries.
questions.a: (a) An official declaration issued by authorities, here by a king. (b) Someone sent on a special mission, often a diplomatic one. Ashoka sent emissaries to Sri Lanka, Thailand or Central Asia.
s: (a) Defines an edict as an official declaration by a king or authority
(b) Defines an emissary and names Sri Lanka, Thailand or Central Asia

questions.q: True or False? 'Ashoka, who ruled from 268 to 232 BCE, was the son of Chandragupta Maurya.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Ashoka (268-232 BCE) was Chandragupta Maurya's grandson, not his son.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: Ashoka was Chandragupta's grandson

questions.q: Neha says: 'Ashoka's concern in his edicts was only for human beings; animals did not matter to him.' Is she right? Give a verdict and two facts from the edicts.
questions.a: No. (1) Ashoka claimed to provide medical care for people and animals, even beyond his empire, and ordered medical treatment for animals when necessary. (2) He prohibited hunting and cruelty to animals, so if his claims are true he was an early contributor to nature conservation and wildlife preservation.
s: Verdict: No
States that he claimed medical care for animals as well as people
States that he prohibited hunting and cruelty to animals

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Historians have sometimes called Ashoka a 'great communicator'.
Reason (R): Ashoka kept his messages on palm leaves written in Sanskrit, stored in his palace at Pataliputra for his officials alone.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: Ashoka is called a great communicator because he had edicts engraved on rocks and pillars in many parts of his empire, mostly in Prakrit, the popular language, so that his messages reached the people.

questions.q: The chapter says that, in line with Kautilya's philosophy of governance, Ashoka paid attention to the welfare of his subjects. (a) State Kautilya's central philosophy of governance in your own words. (b) Give two welfare measures that Ashoka claims in his edicts. (c) Give one instruction from his edict to city magistrates that shows the same philosophy. (d) Give one way in which Ashoka went beyond what the chapter reports of Kautilya's ideas. (e) The chapter warns that we need not take all of Ashoka's claims literally. Does that weaken the link with Kautilya? Give your judgement.
questions.a: (a) The king's happiness lies in the happiness of his subjects; however powerful, he must give first place to the people's interests. (b) Any two: medical care for people and animals; rest houses and wells at regular intervals along main roads; fruit and shade trees planted; encouraging all sects to study each other's best teachings. (c) For example: gain the affection of men and practise impartiality; or see that men are never imprisoned or tortured without good reason, with an officer sent on tour every five years to check. (d) He chose to give up violence after Kalinga and follow the Buddha's path of peace, or cared for animals and banned hunting, whereas Kautilya allowed warfare as well as alliances. (e) It does not break the link: even if some claims are exaggerated, the edicts show what Ashoka wanted to be seen doing, and the chapter judges it clear that he paid attention to his subjects' welfare and tried to reach them, which matches Kautilya's philosophy.
s: (a) States Kautilya's philosophy: the subjects' happiness and welfare come first
(b) Gives two welfare measures from the edicts
(c) Gives one instruction to magistrates (affection, impartiality, no imprisonment without reason)
(d) Gives one way Ashoka went further: non-violence after Kalinga or care for animals
(e) Judges the warning, concluding the link holds because the chapter finds his welfare effort clear

questions.q:
A history club studies a main road of the Maurya Empire 300 km long. Ashoka's edict claims that rest houses and wells were set up at regular intervals along the main roads and that fruit and shade trees were planted. Suppose the claim means a rest house with a well at every 20 km, starting with one at the 0 km mark and ending with one at the 300 km mark. Suppose also that archaeologists surveying this road have found the remains of 11 old wells, each at a point that fits this 20 km pattern.
(a) How many rest houses with wells would the road have if the claim were fully true?
(b) Besides rest houses and wells, what else did Ashoka say was provided along the roads?
(c) Which feature of an empire, from the chapter's list, does this work show?
(d) On a second main road, 240 km long, with the same 20 km pattern from end to end, the survey has found 10 old wells. Which road's survey gives the stronger support to the edict's claim? Decide by working out the percentage of the claimed wells found on each road.
questions.a: (a) 300 / 20 = 15 gaps, so 15 + 1 = 16 rest houses with wells. (b) Fruit and shade trees were planted. (c) The emperor maintains communication networks such as roads and other infrastructure for administration, trade and people's welfare. (d) First road: 11 / 16 x 100 = 68.75%. Second road: 240 / 20 + 1 = 13 claimed wells, and 10 / 13 x 100 = about 76.9%. The second road's survey gives the stronger support, because a larger share of its claimed wells has been found, even though fewer wells were found there in number.
s: (a) Computes 16 rest houses (15 gaps of 20 km plus one)
(b) Names fruit and shade trees
(c) Names the feature: communication networks and infrastructure for trade and people's welfare
(d) Computes 68.75% (11 of 16) and about 76.9% (10 of 13) and decides that the 240 km road gives the stronger support

questions.q: The dharmachakra on the Sarnath lion capital symbolises the Buddha's teachings. Where does the chapter say the dharmachakra is depicted in India today?
o: At the centre of India's national flag
On the India Post stamp that honours Panini
On the Greek coin showing Alexander attacking Porus
questions.a: At the centre of India's national flag.

questions.q: The lion capital that later became India's national emblem was the top of a pillar Ashoka had erected at a place where the Buddha gave his first teaching. Which place is it?
questions.a: Sarnath, near Varanasi.

questions.q: (a) What is the big, round hemispherical structure in the centre of a stupa called, and what does it represent? (b) What is the act of walking around it in a circle as a form of worship called?
questions.a: (a) The anda; it represents the universe and is often built to house sacred relics. (b) Pradakshina.
s: (a) Names the anda and says it represents the universe
(b) Names pradakshina

questions.q:
Read the statements about life in the Mauryan period, as the chapter reports it.
I. Megasthenes' account says that a substantial proportion of the population was engaged in agriculture, an important source of revenue for the empire.
II. Later accounts describe a cotton lower garment reaching below the knee and an upper garment thrown over the shoulders.
III. The Sohagaura copper plate, one of India's earliest administrative records, was discovered at Pataliputra.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements I and II are correct. Statement III is wrong: the Sohagaura copper plate was discovered in Sohgaura, Uttar Pradesh.

questions.q: A visitor's notes on a Mauryan city read: 'The houses are made of wood, some two storeys tall. Vessels of water stand at regular intervals along the streets. The streets have signs, and couriers carry messages from place to place.' (a) Link the first two notes: why would such a city keep water on its streets? (b) What do the street signs and the couriers together show about how the city was run? (c) A pupil says such cities were only for the king and his officials. Correct her using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Wooden houses catch fire easily, so water was kept ready at regular intervals in case of fire. (b) The city was well planned and organised: signs helped people find their way and couriers gave a system of communication. (c) Merchants and artisans also played key roles in city life; blacksmiths, potters, carpenters, jewellers and other artisans lived in the cities.
s: (a) Links wooden houses to the fire risk that the water vessels guard against
(b) States that the cities were well planned, with signage and a courier system of communication
(c) States that merchants and artisans also lived in and played key roles in the cities

questions.q: Each event below happens in a different imaginary empire. For each, name the cause of an empire's decline from the chapter that it shows, and say how it weakens the empire. (a) To pay for a ten-year war in distant hills, an emperor orders every local ruler to send two more elephants and 500 more sacks of grain each year. (b) A famous conqueror dies and his brother, who has lost every battle he fought, takes the throne; a group of hill chieftains holds back its yearly tribute. (c) A border province lies 90 days' march from the capital; news of a revolt there takes a month to reach the emperor, and it is the first province to break away. (d) For two years the sea floods a coastal province, its fields and ports are ruined, and the empire's trade and income collapse.
questions.a: (a) Increasing demands for tribute to pay for a long military campaign burden local rulers and cause resentment, tempting regions to become independent. (b) A powerful emperor followed by one perceived to be weak: local chieftains take a chance and stop paying tribute. (c) Size: the larger an empire, the harder it is to hold together, and far-off territories are often the first to split away. (d) An economic crisis caused by a natural calamity (floods) can shake the empire's structure.
s: (a) Identifies rising tribute demands for a long campaign, leading to resentment
(b) Identifies a successor seen as weak, so chieftains stop paying tribute
(c) Identifies size: far-off territories split away first
(d) Identifies economic crisis from a natural calamity shaking the empire

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter describes empires as fragile at their core and unstable over time.
Reason (R): Empires have almost always been established through war and have kept their existence through force and repression.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the chapter says being built by war and held by force and repression is what makes empires fragile at their core.

questions.q:
Wear the hat of a historian. A school display called 'The Mauryan Legacy' has room for only three exhibits. Five are offered: (P) a punch-marked coin of Ashoka; (Q) a terracotta female deity (yakshi) holding a fly whisk; (R) a terracotta of the Saptamatrikas, the seven mother goddesses; (S) a highly polished Mauryan stone pillar; (T) a written account of Pataliputra as a bustling centre of governance and commerce, with palaces, public buildings and well-planned streets.
(a) Which exhibit is evidence of the extensive use of coins for trade?
(b) The chapter calls the Saptamatrikas terracotta 'a continuing tradition'. What does this tell a historian about the worship of the seven mother goddesses?
(c) Which item of the Mauryan legacy in the chapter's closing summary does exhibit T show? Give one detail from T that supports it.
(d) Exhibits Q, R and S all come under one item of the legacy. Name it.
(e) Choose the three exhibits that together show the largest number of different legacy items, and explain why a choice that includes two of Q, R and S is weaker.
questions.a: (a) P, the punch-marked coin of Ashoka. (b) The tradition did not end with the Mauryas: the worship of the seven mother goddesses carried on in later times. (c) Well-designed urban settlements: for example, the palaces and public buildings, or the well-planned streets. (d) The Mauryas promoted art and architecture. (e) P, T and any one of Q, R or S: they show three different legacy items (coins for trade, well-designed urban settlements, art and architecture). Two of Q, R and S show the same item, art and architecture, so a choice with two of them covers only two legacy items.
s: (a) Names the punch-marked coin of Ashoka (P)
(b) Explains that the worship of the seven mother goddesses carried on after the Mauryas
(c) Names well-designed urban settlements with one supporting detail from T
(d) Names art and architecture
(e) Chooses P, T and one of Q, R, S (three legacy items) and explains that two art exhibits repeat one legacy item
